extracted.intended_audience: NLP and computational-journalism researchers / dataset creators working on media bias and factuality detection (especially for Portuguese)
extracted.subtask_description: Create and annotate a sentence-level dataset and build models to predict whether individual news sentences are factual, biased (by type), or direct quotes; and use these predictions to estimate media-source reliability. Focus is on Brazilian Portuguese news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence-level class scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Each sentence is labeled as one of three classes: (i) factual spans, (ii) biased spans, and (iii) quotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factual = impartial/objective fact-focused; Biased = presents journalist point-of-view or subjectivity and is further classified into bias types; Quotes = direct statements often in quotation marks and treated separately. Use sentence segmentation (spaCy) and annotate each sentence independently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual spans
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Factual spans … a type of information presented with impartiality focused on the objective fact or, in other words, they are sentences that describe a fact and are committed to objectivity.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify as factual when the sentence is committed with impartiality and focuses on objective facts (examples: S2, S4 in paper). Factual spans comprise the majority of sentences (~68.5%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Biased spans
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Biased spans … stray from impartial facts and present the point of view of the journalist …’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a sentence is not impartial/objective, label it biased and then map it to one of the defined bias types (see individual bias-type criteria). In the dataset biased spans are fewer (~8.8% of sentences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Quotes consist of direct statements often followed by quotation marks that journalists in general use to report the speech of someone involved in the reported event.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat quotes as a separate class (neither biased nor factual) — they should not be conflated with journalist-produced bias even if they contain subjective text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotation decision rule: impartiality test
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotators first evaluate whether the sentence is committed with impartiality (i.e., focused on objective facts). If yes → factual; otherwise → biased (and assign bias subtype) or quote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow this binary decision flow as the primary annotation heuristic; use AllSides guidelines for defining bias types and provide examples to annotators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spin
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘This type of bias consists of vague, dramatic, or sensational language.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect words implying subjective interpretation (example: ‘gloated’ indicates subjective interpretation). Label sentences using dramatic/sensational framing as Spin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unsubstantiated Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘This bias occurs when journalists provide claims in their reporting without including any evidence.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label sentences that assert claims without supporting evidence or attribution (example given: claims about condemnation without backing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinion Statements Presented as Facts
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Journalists use subjective language or statements under the guise of reporting objectively, which is based on personal opinions, assumptions, beliefs, tastes, preferences, or interpretations.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark sentences that present subjective judgments as factual statements (example: interpretation of policy effects presented as fact).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensationalism/Emotionalism
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Here, the information is presented in a way that provides a shock or triggers a deep impression.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label sentences that use shock-inducing phrasing or emotional framing (example: phrasing implying a ‘bloodbath’).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mudslinging/Ad Hominem
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘This type of media bias occurs when unfair or insulting things are said about someone in order to damage their reputation.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotate sentences containing insulting, reputation-damaging language targeting individuals (example: name-calling).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mind Reading
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘This bias occurs when journalists assume they know what another person thinks, or thinks that the way they see the world reflects the way the world really is.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label sentences that ascribe unverified thoughts, intentions, or emotions to others (example: saying a politician ‘hates’ or ‘is convinced’ without evidence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Flowed Logic
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘This bias consists of a type of faulty reasoning resulting in misrepresenting people’s opinions or arriving at conclusions that are not justified by the given evidence.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify sentences that contain non sequitur reasoning or unjustified inferences and mark as Flowed Logic (example: drawing an unwarranted conclusion from unrelated premises).

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of Source Attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘This bias occurs when a journalist does not back up their claims by linking to the source of that information.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotate sentences that refer vaguely to ‘critics say’ or similar without specific attribution or evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective Qualifying Adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Journalists can reveal this bias when they include subjective, qualifying adjectives in front of specific words or phrases.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag sentences that use subjective qualifiers (e.g., ‘sinister’, ‘extremist’) that insert the journalist’s evaluation instead of objective description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word Choice
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘This bias occurs when words and phrases are loaded with political implications. Therefore, the words or phrases a media outlet uses can reveal its perspective or ideology.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label sentences where lexicon choices (‘riot’ vs ‘protest’, ‘illegal immigrants’ vs ‘migrants’) indicate framing; consider lexicon-level polarization signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negativity Bias
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Journalists can emphasize bad or negative news, or frame events in a negative light.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark sentences that emphasize negative framing or disproportionately stress negative aspects to attract attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elite v. Populist Bias
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Journalists can defer to the beliefs, viewpoints, and perspectives of people who are part of society’s most prestigious or not prestigious … journalist pushes back against the elite government, saying they can’t be trusted.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotate sentences that frame issues in terms of elite vs populist perspectives or that explicitly elevate/devalue elites or popular groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excluded AllSides bias types for sentence-level annotation
rubrics_metrics.description: The authors did not consider four AllSides types — slant, bias by omission, bias by story choice, and photo bias — because they did not match the sentence-level proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply these four types at sentence level in this annotation schema; they are considered document- or editorial-level phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotator profile and qualification
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotators comprised two individuals (a linguist and a computer scientist) from different regions, both with at least a Ph.D. degree or Ph.D. candidate status; annotation was led by an NLP researcher and supported by the annotation schema and AllSides guideline examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use at-least-expert annotators (linguist/media-bias expert + non-expert) with oversight; provide the annotators with the schema and rich examples to improve reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjudication and inter-annotator agreement practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute inter-annotator agreement (Cohen’s kappa) and adjudicate disagreements via judges and meetings; reported kappa = 0.82.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Cohen’s kappa to quantify agreement; resolve disagreements with judges and multiple discussion meetings; aim for high diagonal agreement in confusion matrix and document disagreement cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data collection: same-story triple sampling
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect the same news story from three different media outlets (here: Folha, O Globo, Estadão) to form article triples; the dataset contains 100 stories × 3 outlets = 300 documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When estimating outlet-level reliability, sample identical stories across outlets to control for topic differences and allow cross-outlet comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain and temporal sampling constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect across six domains (politics, world, daily, sports, science, culture) and two periods (2006–2007 and 2021–2022).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure cross-domain coverage and temporal diversity to avoid domain/time-specific bias in dataset; the dataset reported domain proportions (e.g., 62.55% politics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preprocessing and sentence segmentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Segment articles into sentences using spaCy and remove only special characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reliable sentence segmentation tools; minimal cleaning preserves linguistic cues important for bias detection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class balancing and sampling during modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply undersampling to balance classes (as done for some experiments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When training binary classifiers with imbalanced labels, use undersampling or other balancing techniques to avoid bias towards majority class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train/test split and validation protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: Split data into train (90%) and test (10%) and apply 10-fold cross-validation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use held-out test sets and cross-validation to estimate generalization; document folds and random seeds for reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation metrics: precision, recall, F1-Score
rubrics_metrics.description: Report precision, recall, and F1-Score for models; baseline reported F1: factuality 0.88 (best), media bias 0.67 (best).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use standard classification metrics per-class and macro/micro as appropriate; present comparisons with prior datasets and baselines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model architectures and feature sets to test
rubrics_metrics.description: Test multiple architectures/feature sets: BERT fine-tuning (hyperparams: batch_size=64, lr=2e-05, epochs=4), subjective-lexicons (BoW with sentiment/emotion lexicons), part-of-speech BoW (noun/verb/adjective/adverb/pronoun/conjunction), TF-IDF, emotion-lexicon features; SVM with linear kernel used as learning method in some experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare contextualized models (BERT) with linguistically-motivated feature-based baselines (POS, lexicons, TF-IDF); report hyperparameters and setups for reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of sentence-level media bias modeling task
rubrics_metrics.description: Binary classification: biased spans vs unbiased spans (balanced set used: 558 biased vs 558 unbiased labels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define positive class clearly; for evaluation, use balanced test sets or report class-imbalanced metrics; note that biased spans are relatively infrequent in natural distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of sentence-level factuality modeling task
rubrics_metrics.description: Binary classification where biased spans + quotes are grouped as non-factual vs factual spans (balanced used: 1,949 vs 1,949 labels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When predicting factuality, consider quotes as non-factual for modeling purposes; ensure the class grouping is documented and justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset size and class distribution standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Dataset contains 6,191 sentences: 4,302 factual, 1,389 quotes, 558 biased. Average words per sentence: factual 20.36, biased 22.14, quotes 17.38.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document class counts, averages, and distribution across body/title and domains; use these statistics to inform sampling, baseline expectations, and evaluation interpretation.
